To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

women diagnosed with an eating disorder report experiencing both pleasant and unpleasant emotions more frequently and more intensely than do controls, and that the pattern of relationships among pleasant emotion, eating-disorder themes, and belief-systems is distinct from that of unpleasant emotion.

women diagnosed with an eating disorder reported experiencing both positive and negative emotion more frequently than do women in the control group; that pleasant emotions correlated more highly with eating disorder themes in the eating disordered women than in the control group, and that maladaptive schema were more highly associated with pleasant than unpleasant emotion experience in the eating-disorder group.
eating disorders are associated with the experience of positive as well as negative emotions, and the regulation of positive emotions is a significant factor in the maintenance of these disorders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how emotion experience and regulation are related to the development and maintenance of eating disorders.
the role of emotion in the development and maintenance of eating disorders.
the relationship between emotional experience and psychological processes in women diagnosed with eating disorder.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the regulation of both positive and negatively toned emotions may be important in the development and maintenance of eating disorders.
women with eating disordered behaviors are not only experiencing more negative emotions, but they are also experiencing more positive emotions than women without disordered eating behaviors.
eating disorder behaviors are not just about the management of negative emotion, but also about positive emotion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
eating-disordered women are more emotionally sensitive and experience both pleasant and unpleasant emotions more frequently, but are not necessarily more distressed than nonclinical women.
the regulation of both pleasant and unpleasant emotions is disrupted in eating-disordered individuals, and that this disruption may be related to the use of eating disorder behaviors.

women with eating disorder experience a wide range of emotions, and use their eating disorder to manage their experience of both negative and positive emotions, but that the pattern of associations between emotion and eating disorder themes is quite different for eating disordered women than for controls.
The main takeaway from our work is that
eating disorders are not simply about avoiding negative emotions.
the eating disorder patient is not a passive recipient of emotion, but rather an active agent who is capable of regulating her emotional experience in a variety of ways, some of them maladaptive.
it is essential to study the experience of both negative and positive emotions in clinical populations.
